361.quote_or_event: “Some are happy, and some are sad. Caught in the desires of the mind, they perish.”
361.explanation: Guru Nanak says that people, whether happy or sad, are destroyed by being caught in the desires and attachments of the mind.
361.tie_back: The Kural calls desire the seed that unfailingly produces birth after birth; Guru Nanak says desire is what destroys people, though he does not here call it the seed of rebirth.
361.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 152, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
361._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Gurbani links moh and trishna to death and rebirth elsewhere, but no verified verse found calls desire the seed of birth, and this line speaks only of perishing.

362.quote_or_event: “In the midst of hope, the Guru teaches us to live above hope and desire.”
362.explanation: Guru Nanak says the Guru teaches a person to live among hopes and wants while remaining free of them.
362.tie_back: The Kural turns desire against itself, asking us to desire freedom from desire; Guru Nanak's niraas, being free of hope in the midst of hope, is the same paradox lived out.
362.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 154, Raag Gauree, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
362._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on transcending desire from within; Gurbani frames it as the Guru's teaching for life in the world, not as a desire for non-birth.

363.quote_or_event: “Without contentment, no one is satisfied. Like the objects in a dream, all his efforts are in vain. Through the love of the Naam, all peace is obtained.”
363.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan says that without contentment nothing satisfies, and that every kind of peace is found in love of the Name.
363.tie_back: The Kural calls freedom from desire the choicest wealth in this world and the next; Guru Arjan says that without contentment no possession satisfies and that all peace comes from the Name.
363.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
363._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on contentment as the true treasure; Guru Arjan locates the highest good in the Name rather than in desirelessness itself.

364.quote_or_event: “They are not called pure, who sit down after merely washing their bodies. Only they are pure, O Nanak, within whose minds the Lord abides.”
364.explanation: In Asa di Vaar Guru Nanak rejects ritual bathing as the test of purity and says only those in whose minds God dwells are pure.
364.tie_back: The Kural defines purity as freedom from desire rather than bathing, diet or caste rule; Guru Nanak likewise moves purity from the washed body to the inner mind.
364.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 472, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
364._accuracy_note: A strong fit on inner rather than ritual purity; Guru Nanak defines purity by God's presence in the mind, while the Kural defines it as the absence of craving born of longing for truth.

365.quote_or_event: “When you abandon hope and desire, then you become a true Sannyaasi.”
365.explanation: Guru Nanak redefines the renunciant: the true sannyasi is not one who wears the robe but one who has given up hope and desire.
365.tie_back: The Kural says only those who have cut off desire deserve to be called true renunciants, whatever else others have given up; Guru Nanak says exactly this.
365.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 356, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
365._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one; Guru Nanak uses the definition to reject outward asceticism in favour of inner freedom while living in the world.

366.quote_or_event: “Maya is a serpent, clinging to the world. Whoever serves her, she ultimately devours.”
366.explanation: Guru Amar Das calls Maya, the lure of worldly desire, a serpent wrapped around the world that in the end devours those who serve it.
366.tie_back: The Kural says that to fear desire is itself virtue because desire deceives and ruins; Guru Amar Das gives that fear its reason, a serpent that destroys its own servants.
366.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 510, Raag Gujri (Gujri ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
366._accuracy_note: A strong fit on desire as a deceiver that ruins; the Kural speaks of desire itself, Guru Amar Das of Maya, the world's allure that feeds it.

367.quote_or_event: “who renounces all hopes and desires and remains desireless in the world; who is not touched by sexual desire or anger - within his heart, God dwells.”
367.explanation: Guru Tegh Bahadur describes the person who has given up all hopes and desires and is untouched by lust and anger; in that heart God dwells, and the hymn ends with such a person merging in God like water in water.
367.tie_back: The Kural promises that one who cuts off desire completely will gain the deeds that lead to undying life; Guru Tegh Bahadur promises that the desireless heart becomes God's dwelling.
367.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 633, Raag Sorath, Guru Tegh Bahadur (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
367._accuracy_note: A strong thematic fit on total desirelessness bringing the highest good; the Sikh reward is God's indwelling and merger, not a promise of imperishable deeds.

368.quote_or_event: “The fire of desire is deep within; unsatisfied, people remain hungry and thirsty.”
368.explanation: Guru Angad says that desire is a fire burning inside, and that those who carry it stay hungry and thirsty however much they get.
368.tie_back: The Kural says that where desire exists sorrow comes without fail, one upon another; Guru Angad describes the same endless hunger and thirst that desire brings.
368.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 138, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Angad (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
368._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: it shows desire producing continual suffering, but does not state the Kural's converse that those without desire have no sorrow.

369.quote_or_event: “The mind and body are cooled and soothed; peace ensues, and the fire of desire is quenched.”
369.explanation: Guru Amar Das says that through the Guru's Word the fire of desire is put out and body and mind become cool and peaceful.
369.tie_back: The Kural says that when desire, the sorrow of sorrows, is destroyed, joy flows without break even in this life; Guru Amar Das describes the peace that follows once desire's fire is quenched.
369.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 588, Raag Vadhans (Vadhans ki Vaar, salok), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
369._accuracy_note: A strong fit on peace in this life once desire is quenched; the Kural stresses unbroken joy, Gurbani a cooling peace given through the Guru's Word.

370.quote_or_event: “Earning a thousand, he runs after a hundred thousand. Satisfaction is not obtained by chasing after Maya.”
370.explanation: In Sukhmani Guru Arjan shows the endless escalation of wanting: every gain only starts the chase for more, and no satisfaction comes from Maya.
370.tie_back: The Kural says desire by nature can never be filled; Guru Arjan pictures exactly that insatiable nature, and the same passage goes on to place lasting peace in the Name.
370.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 278-279, Raag Gauree, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
370._accuracy_note: A strong fit on desire's insatiable nature; the Kural's promised unchanging bliss is found in Sikhism through the Name rather than through casting off desire as such.
